title: Boss tests, pass marks, and when to hold a child back
lede: How the ten boss tests work, how to read a failed part, and how to tell a parent "not yet" without losing the child.
mirrors: the boss test at the end of every stage in the trainer

sections.title: Video script
sections.html:
Video script

Every stage ends with a boss. You've seen three of them. Today you learn how all ten work, how to read a fail, and when to hold a child back.

What a boss is

A boss is a short timed test in two to four parts. No hints. The child has to pass every part to open the next stage. Pass, and they earn the stage badge.

Each part maps to one or two lessons. That's the whole design. When a part fails, you know which lessons to go back to. You never have to guess.

Proven programs do the same thing. UCMAS grades every level with an exam. The franchise programs give a certificate per level, and they grade accuracy before speed. Our boss is that grade, once a stage.

The ten bosses

On screenthe ten boss cards, one at a time

Sprout: read hundreds, set hundreds, and direct problems of three lines.

Explorer: ten single-rod "friend or free?" moves, 2-digit problems of four lines, and a mental round of three small numbers.

Apprentice: ten carry-or-borrow moves, 2-digit problems of five lines, and a mental round of four 1-digit numbers.

Adept: ten combination moves, 3-digit problems of five lines, and a mental round of three 2-digit numbers.

Ace: 3-digit problems ten lines long, five-line mental problems with two digits, and flash: eight 1-digit numbers at one second.

Wizard: twenty times tables in a minute, then 3-digit by 1-digit, 2-digit by 2-digit, and a mental 2-digit by 1-digit round.

Champion: 3-digit by 1-digit division, 4-digit by 2-digit division, mental division, and 2-digit flash at 0.7 seconds.

Prodigy: all mental. Ten 3-digit lines, 3-digit flash, 2-digit by 2-digit, and division.

Grandmaster: dan-level targets. Ten 3-digit numbers flashed at half a second, 4-digit mental lines, and mental multiply and divide.

Legend: fifteen 3-digit numbers flashed at 0.3 seconds, and 3-digit by 3-digit in the head. That one's for the record.

Pass marks

The pass marks sit between 75 and 90 percent. Single-rod parts need nine of ten, because those are pure decisions with no arithmetic to slip on. Most written parts need five of six. The long ten-line and four-digit parts need three of four.

On screenDecision parts 90% · Most parts 80–83% · Long parts 75%

The clock matters, but it's generous. A child who is accurate rarely runs out of time.

Bosses take two or three tries

Tell every parent this before the first boss. Bosses are meant to take two or three tries. A fail is information, not a verdict.

Here's what you say to the child. "The boss is just the lessons, in a row, with a clock." That's all it is.

Reading a fail

Look at which part failed. Then go back to the lessons that part maps to. Three days on those lessons. Then try the boss again.

Say the Apprentice boss fails on part two, the five-line problems, but parts one and three pass. The moves are fine. The child is losing it across five lines. Go back to "Borrow chains and mixed problems" for three days.

Now say part one fails, the single carry-or-borrow moves. That's a decision problem. Go back to the big-friend lessons, and slow down.

Then look at the size of the misses. Off by exactly five is a heaven bead. Off by ten is a lost carry or a lost borrow. We go deep on that in Lesson 19.

When to hold a child back

Holding back means not opening the next stage yet. The boss does most of that for you. But watch for these signs, even after a pass.

The lesson drills aren't passing three days running. The child is counting beads one at a time. Accuracy holds only at a crawl. Or the child is anxious about the beads.

If any of those is true, stay in the stage. Repeat the drills. It costs a week. Moving a child up too early costs a stage.

And never test a child who is tired, sick or upset. One try a day is enough. Two fails in one evening teaches a child to dread the boss.

Under six

For kids under six, expect the first two stages to take twice as long. Ten-minute sessions. If reading numbers hasn't clicked after a month, pause for a few months and come back.

Telling a parent

Never say "failed." Say "not yet," and say what's next. "She passed two parts. Part two is the five-line problems. We'll do three days of that lesson and try again Saturday."

A parent who hears a plan doesn't worry. A parent who hears "failed" does.

sections.title: Drill set
sections.html:
Drill set

A. Mark a practice boss sheet: Explorer, part 2

The child answers are made up for this drill. Work each problem, mark it right or wrong, then decide: pass or not yet? The pass mark is 5 of 6 (83%).

  1. 28 − 24 + 53 + 31 · child wrote 88
  2. 78 + 21 − 81 − 17 · child wrote 6
  3. 37 + 62 − 12 − 23 · child wrote 64
  4. 59 − 17 + 53 − 23 · child wrote 72
  5. 49 + 50 − 10 − 47 · child wrote 42
  6. 98 − 81 + 31 − 45 · child wrote 8

B. Mark a practice boss sheet: Apprentice, part 2

Same job. Pass mark 5 of 6.

  1. 65 + 13 − 46 + 95 − 48 · child wrote 79
  2. 11 + 60 + 45 + 30 + 40 · child wrote 186
  3. 18 + 30 + 92 + 17 − 81 · child wrote 86
  4. 92 + 77 − 52 + 44 − 55 · child wrote 106
  5. 48 − 20 + 20 + 37 − 75 · child wrote 10
  6. 78 − 55 + 71 + 69 + 35 · child wrote 198

sections.title: Teach-back
sections.html:
Teach-back

Take your marked sheet from section A. Write the message you would send the parent: two to four sentences, no word "failed", the part that missed, the lesson you will go back to, and the day you will retry. Then say it out loud to a partner playing the parent, and let them ask one worried question. Write your answer to that question.

sections.title: Check: five questions
sections.html:
Check: five questions

  1. What are the three rules every boss follows?
  2. Why do single-rod boss parts need nine of ten?
  3. An Explorer boss: parts one and three pass, part two fails. What do you do?
  4. Name four signs that a child should stay in a stage even after a pass.
  5. Rewrite this message: "Sam failed the Apprentice boss."

sections.title: Answers
sections.html:
Answers

Drill answers

A. 1) 88, right · 2) 1, wrong (off by 5) · 3) 64, right · 4) 72, right · 5) 42, right · 6) 3, wrong (off by 5). Verdict: 4 of 6, not yet

B. 1) 79, right · 2) 186, right · 3) 76, wrong (off by 10) · 4) 106, right · 5) 10, right · 6) 198, right. Verdict: 5 of 6, pass

Check answers

  1. Timed, no hints, and every part must pass to open the next stage.
  2. They test pure decisions, with no arithmetic to slip on.
  3. Go back to the 2-digit small-friend lessons ("All eight friends, mixed" and the speed round) for three days, then retry.
  4. Lesson drills not passing three days running. Counting beads one at a time. Accuracy only at a crawl. Anxiety about the beads.
  5. For example: "Sam passed two of the three parts. Part two, the five-line problems, is next. We'll spend three days on that lesson and try again Saturday."
